title: A Room for the Hymn
premise: Bram Brightwater has worked hospice wards for a decade, comforting the dying while quietly enduring the backwards counting only they can hear—a hymn sung in reverse by something patient beneath the town of Hollowmere. When an excavation crew unearths a door sealed from the inside, the counting stops, and the thing that sang begins looking for a voice to carry its final verse. Bram discovers they are descended from the Brightwaters who built the seal and abandoned the song unfinished, leaving their heirs as the only possible singers. To end it, Bram must learn the hymn's last verse from the dying themselves and choose whether to sing it forward—binding the thing forever at the cost of their own voice, their memories, and the fragile belonging they've finally found.
about_author: Cyrus Sandoval is the pen name of a former hospice volunteer who spent three years in rural Appalachia collecting funeral hymns before turning to horror. They write in longhand at night and claim they have never once heard the counting.

chapters.title: The Counting Ward
chapters.summary: Bram, POV throughout, works the night shift at Hollowmere Hospice, where each dying patient counts down in a whisper they shouldn't be able to hear through walls. Bram soothes them with routines and small kindnesses, telling themselves the counting is grief-shaped coincidence. Emotional beat: lonely competence—the reader sees how hard Bram works to belong to a world that explains everything.

chapters.title: What the Excavator Found
chapters.summary: A construction crew breaks ground on the hospice expansion and strikes a stone door sealed from the inside, its surface carved with musical notation no one can read. That night the counting stops mid-number, and every patient wakes at once. Bram's POV, dread building. Emotional beat: the safety of rational explanation begins to crack.

chapters.title: Ten Years of Noises
chapters.summary: In flashback braided with present scenes, Bram recalls childhood nights in the Brightwater farmhouse—the same backwards counting, a grandmother who salted doorways and forbade humming. Bram's estranged aunt Odile arrives uninvited, saying the door changes things. Emotional beat: the past Bram buried resurfaces, and inheritance stops being abstract.

chapters.title: The Verse in the Walls
chapters.summary: Patients begin humming fragments of a melody none of them know, and the hospice's oldest resident, Mrs. Ellery, sings a verse forward for the first time before dying peacefully—too peacefully. Bram realizes the dying aren't counting down; they're rehearsing. Emotional beat: horror sharpened by tenderness, as Bram cares for people becoming instruments.

chapters.title: Odile's Ledger
chapters.summary: Odile reveals the Brightwater family ledger: generations who maintained the seal by singing the hymn forward at each deathbed, feeding it voices until the line thinned and the practice was abandoned. The door was sealed from the inside by the last singer, who locked the thing in with herself. Emotional beat: Bram's anger at the family's cowardice, and fear that they are the spare part.

chapters.title: The Town That Forgot to Sing
chapters.summary: Hollowmere's history surfaces: a century of vanished choirs, a church with a bricked-over choir loft, townspeople who flinch at hymns. Bram interviews the town archivist, who goes silent mid-sentence and starts counting that night. Emotional beat: isolation deepens—Bram sees the whole town has survived by not listening.

chapters.title: Doors Sealed From the Inside
chapters.summary: Bram descends to the excavation at night and presses an ear to the door, hearing the hymn sung backward by many voices—including, horribly, their grandmother's. The thing has been keeping the dead, learning from every Brightwater it swallowed. Emotional beat: grief weaponized; Bram understands the enemy knows them intimately.

chapters.title: The Last Verse
chapters.summary: Odile, dying of the illness she hid, teaches Bram the final verse—the binding that the family never finished because it requires a singer to give up their voice and every memory of belonging. Bram refuses, and Odile sings it alone, buying days, not salvation. Emotional beat: love and fury entwined; the price becomes real and personal.

chapters.title: Singing Along
chapters.summary: The door opens. The hospice fills with the backwards hymn, patients and staff falling into chorus, and only Bram—half-deaf to it by inheritance—can walk the corridor unclaimed. Bram reaches the threshold and begins the final verse forward, the thing singing along, trying to twist it backward mid-phrase. Climax: Bram must finish the verse while the memory of everyone they love is pulled from them note by note.

chapters.title: A Room for the Hymn
chapters.summary: Bram completes the verse; the seal closes with the thing inside and the song finally finished, silent at last. Bram survives but cannot remember faces—only that they were loved, and that they chose this. The hospice patients die in ordinary silence. Final beat: bittersweet resolution—Bram has paid for belonging with the memory of it, and stays anyway.
